title: Faith the seed
hook: a brahmin farmer with five hundred plows tells the Buddha to plow for his food
carry: plant one seed you can't see

segments.voice: Yesterday: sahaya, the wise companion, and your line, we praise the blessing of companionship. Today ends the week, out in a field at sowing time.

Sowing day on a big farm in Magadha. A brahmin named Kasi Bharadvaja has five hundred plows out in his fields, and at lunchtime he's handing out food to the workers. A man with a bowl walks up and stands quietly at the edge of the line. The farmer isn't impressed. I plow and I sow, he says, and then I eat. You should plow and sow too, and then you can eat. It's a fair point, the kind people still make about anyone whose work you can't see. The Buddha's answer is today's poem.
screen: `FIVE HUNDRED PLOWS AT SOWING TIME.` → `I PLOW, THEN I EAT.` → `YOU SHOULD TOO.`

segments.voice: The Buddha says: I plow and sow too, brahmin, and then I eat. The farmer is puzzled: we don't see your yoke, your plow, your oxen. So the Buddha describes his farm, in verse. Faith is the seed. Discipline is the rain. Wisdom is my yoke and plow. Conscience is the pole, the mind the strap, mindfulness my plowshare and goad. Guarded in body and speech, moderate in food. Truth is how I weed. Effort is my ox, pulling toward freedom without turning back. And this plowing has the deathless as its harvest. Notice where faith sits: it's the seed, the very first thing, put into the ground before anything shows. Saddha, the Pali word, can be translated faith, trust or confidence. Here it isn't the harvest. It's the trust that gets you to begin. Then wisdom and effort and mindfulness do the work. The farmer is moved and offers milk-rice in a bronze bowl. The Buddha declines: food given in payment for verses isn't for him. In the end the farmer asks to go forth. That closes the week, too. A whole collection closed, the oldest poems opened: a snake shedding its skin, a herdsman in the rain, a rhinoceros alone, a friend on the road, and now a field. Each sets an ordinary picture beside a deeper one.
screen: `I PLOW AND SOW TOO` · `FAITH THE SEED, WISDOM THE PLOW` · `TRUST THAT GETS YOU TO BEGIN` · `A WEEK OF ORDINARY PICTURES` · then, large: `FAITH THE SEED.`

segments.voice: Quietly name your own farm: your seed, the small trust that got you started on something good; your plow, the steady tool you use, like patience, honesty or an early alarm; your ox, the effort that keeps pulling. Then let the breath be the slow work of a field, nothing to force, just showing up.
saddha. The Buddha's farming poem: trust is the seed you plant first, then wisdom plows, effort pulls, and the harvest is freedom. Today's word.
Your line: plant one seed you can't see. Trust starts it; wisdom and effort grow it. See you tomorrow.

howItsDone: Theravada monastics live on alms and do not farm or handle money; lay supporters offer food, and the Kasibharadvaja poem is one text teachers use to explain how monastic and lay life support each other.

options: I plow and sow too, and then I eat.
fork.reveal: he agrees with the farmer's principle, then shows a farm of faith, wisdom, effort and mindfulness.

original.note: Pali saddha: faith, trust, confidence. in Sn 1.4, the seed.

trapdoor: what you thought: faith means believing without evidence.
what it means: in this poem faith is the seed, the trust that gets you to begin, with wisdom and effort doing the work after.
what a scholar hears: saddha is also rendered confidence; some early texts link it to a teacher one has tested, and the Kasibharadvaja Sutta appears in both the Sutta Nipata and the Samyutta Nikaya.
guess: faith, trust, the confidence to begin
proof that removes every doubt for good
a reward paid out for good deeds

chat.says: In that farming poem, where does faith fit in?
options: It's the seed: the trust you plant first, then wisdom and effort work.
It's the harvest: the reward that comes at the very end of the path.
It's the rain: what falls on the field once the plowing is all done.
chat.meaning: In the Buddha's farming poem faith is the seed, planted first. Wisdom is the plow, effort the ox, and the harvest is the deathless.

Magadha.meaning: an old kingdom in northern India

Kasi Bharadvaja.meaning: the brahmin farmer with five hundred plows

brahmin.meaning: a member of the old priestly class

deathless.meaning: freedom beyond death: the harvest of the path

sources.ref: Sutta Nipata 1.4, Kasibharadvaja Sutta (also Samyutta Nikaya 7.11)

notes: Sn 1.4 paraphrased. Confirm the mapping: faith the seed, austerity or discipline (tapo) the rain, wisdom the yoke and plow, conscience (hiri) the pole, mind the strap, mindfulness the plowshare and goad, truth the weeding, energy the ox; the deathless as fruit.
Confirm 'five hundred plows', the setting near Ekanala in Magadha, and the milk-rice offered in a bronze bowl and declined as 'food chanted over with verses'.
The poem's ending also includes the declined food thrown into water, which hisses; omitted here for time.
